1.explanation: The misclassification of a regex literal as a comment start originates in hasPunctuatorBefore(), which looks backward for a punctuator token to decide whether a lone “/” begins a RegExp or denotes division. Because the PUNCTUATOR_REGEX constant does not include the “case” keyword, hasPunctuatorBefore() mistakes the slash after “case” as division, then finds “//” and treats the rest as a comment. Updating PUNCTUATOR_REGEX to include “case” and thereby ensuring hasPunctuatorBefore() recognizes that context is the core of the fix.
1.bug_scenario: When running Lighthouse’s “Minify JavaScript” audit against a script that uses a switch statement with a regex in a case clause (e.g. switch(true){case /^hello!/.test("hello!"):document.write("///<any content>");}), Lighthouse incorrectly treats the code after the first “/” as a comment, marking the file as unminified even though it is minified.

2.explanation: The root of the bug is in minification-estimator.js. The PUNCTUATOR_REGEX constant defines which tokens count as ’punctuators’ before a slash to identify it as a regex start. It omits the keyword `case`, so `hasPunctuatorBefore` misclassifies the slash after `case` as a division operator rather than a regex delimiter. That mistake then causes the subsequent `//` to be parsed as a comment, making the remainder of the file invisible to the tokenizer and leading Lighthouse to believe the file is not minified. Adding `case` to PUNCTUATOR_REGEX or otherwise adjusting hasPunctuatorBefore to treat `case` as a valid punctuator fixes the detection logic.
2.bug_scenario: In Lighthouse DevTools, the “Minify JavaScript” audit flags a fully-minified script as unminified. A small switch/case snippet with a regex literal (`/^hello!/.test("hello!")`) gets misparsed: the slash after “case” is seen as a division, then the next “//” is taken as the start of a comment, so the rest of the code is dropped. The audit then thinks the file is unminified and reports large savings (e.g. ~14 KiB) even though the code is already compressed.
